name: IDP Essentials
description: A foundational baseline practice for Internal Developer Platforms that establishes the universal concerns, activity spaces, competencies, and narrative frameworks governing how organizations design, build, operate, and evolve developer-centric platform capabilities.

focuses.name: Value
focuses.description: Business justification, stakeholder alignment, financial management, risk governance, and the economic case for developer productivity investment through internal developer platforms.

focuses.name: Solution
focuses.description: The technical architecture, developer interfaces, consumption experiences, and workloads that constitute the internal developer platform and the requirements it must satisfy.

focuses.name: Endeavor
focuses.description: The organizational structure, team topology, governance framework, operational practices, and change management required to build, operate, and evolve the internal developer platform.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: Enforces a strict cause-and-effect relationship between context and outcomes. In the IDP context, used for tactical execution reporting (platform capability delivery), incident reviews (platform reliability), capability demonstrations (golden path showcases), and developer experience improvement stories (before/after metrics).

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The starting state before platform intervention.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the developer experience baseline, cognitive load distribution, or delivery performance metrics before platform action is taken. Quantify where possible (e.g., "300 engineers spending 45 minutes/day on infrastructure tasks," "average provisioning time: 3 days," "DORA metrics at Medium level").

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific platform challenge or developer need to address.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Frame the task through the developer experience lens: what cognitive load source, self-service gap, feedback loop bottleneck, or security friction needs to be resolved? Reference specific DevEx dimension (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state).

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The platform intervention or capability delivered.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the platform engineering activities performed, golden paths created, abstractions built, or governance mechanisms implemented. Include the design rationale and TVP decisions. Specify the architectural approach and technology choices.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The measurable outcome and value delivered.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Quantify results using IDP metrics: DORA improvement (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate), developer time saved, adoption rate achieved, NPS change, cost optimization realized, cognitive load shift. Connect platform action to business outcome.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: Effective for macro-level IDP lifecycle orchestrations, particularly the organizational transformation from project-based infrastructure to product-oriented platform engineering. Used for overall baseline narrative, organizational change stories, and multi-year platform evolution narratives.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The pre-platform state of the organization.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the current developer experience: cognitive load distribution (typical 35/45/20 intrinsic/extraneous/germane), manual provisioning processes, infrastructure bottlenecks, team frustration, shadow IT proliferation. Quantify the developer productivity cost using measured data.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the trigger: competitive pressure, AI adoption needs, developer retention crisis, digital transformation mandate, industry peer benchmarking. Reference industry data (Gartner projections, DORA research, CNCF adoption trends).

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the adoption challenges honestly: organizational resistance, J-Curve performance dip, cultural transformation from project to product mindset, team topology redesign, golden path development iteration, enabling team facilitation, and the time required for cultural change to take root.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The new operational reality with realized value.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the transformed organization: self-service platform with high adoption, reduced cognitive load (target 50/15/35), elite DORA metrics, developer satisfaction exceeding targets, platform as strategic asset and AI enablement layer. Quantify the ROI and competitive advantage gained.

narrativeTypes.name: The Three-Act Structure and StoryBrand
narrativeTypes.description: Positions the developer as the Hero and the platform engineering team as the Guide. Used for platform-as-a-product positioning, internal marketing to developer audiences, stakeholder communication, and golden path adoption stories.

narrativeElements.name: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeElements.description: Identifying the developer and their friction.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the primary developer persona (the Hero) and detail their specific cognitive load burden, infrastructure friction, or productivity impediment. Use DevEx research data to make the problem concrete and relatable. Name the specific pain: "provisioning takes 3 days," "security review blocks deployment for 2 weeks," "debugging requires understanding Kubernetes internals."

narrativeElements.name: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeElements.description: The platform team offers a solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Position the platform engineering team as the Guide who provides golden paths, self-service capabilities, and automated governance. Present the plan as the Thinnest Viable Platform that addresses the Hero's specific needs. Emphasize that the platform is optional and compelling, not mandatory. The plan should feel like a gift, not an imposition.

narrativeElements.name: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the call to action (onboarding program, enabling team facilitation, first golden path project) and the successful outcome: reduced cognitive load, faster delivery, higher satisfaction, ecosystem contribution. Document the transformation from reluctant consumer to active contributor.

narrativeTypes.name: Platform Maturity Journey
narrativeTypes.description: A progressive maturity narrative framework designed specifically for IDP contexts, structured around the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model's four levels and the principle that maturity progression is a deliberate investment decision, not a linear march toward perfection. Used for platform strategy communication, maturity assessment reporting, and investment justification.

narrativeElements.name: Current State Assessment
narrativeElements.description: Honest evaluation of where the organization stands across platform maturity dimensions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Assess the current state across the five CNCF maturity aspects (Investment, Adoption, Interfaces, Operations, Measurement) at four levels (Provisional, Operational, Scalable, Optimizing). Reference industry benchmarks: only 13.1% reach Optimizing, 45.5% operate at Operational, 29.6% do not measure success. Be honest about maturity gaps without judgment -- most organizations have uneven maturity across aspects.

narrativeElements.name: Target State Rationale
narrativeElements.description: The justified target maturity level and investment case for each dimension.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the target maturity level per aspect with explicit investment rationale. Apply the CNCF guidance: "reaching the highest level should not be a goal in itself." Justify each target level with expected ROI, developer impact, and organizational readiness. Some aspects may legitimately target different levels based on organizational context and strategy.

narrativeElements.name: Investment and Journey
narrativeElements.description: The progressive steps, investment requirements, and expected trajectory including the J-Curve.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the maturity progression path with realistic timelines. Address the DORA J-Curve: expect initial gains, followed by a complexity dip, before higher performance recovery. Detail the investment required (people, funding, organizational change) at each progression step. Identify quick wins for early momentum and long-term investments for sustained value.

narrativeElements.name: Measurement and Course Correction
narrativeElements.description: How progress is tracked, risks monitored, and plans adjusted based on evidence.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the metrics that validate maturity progression (DORA metrics, adoption rate, DXI, cost efficiency, CNCF maturity self-assessment). Establish measurement cadence and reporting. Guard against Goodhart's Law with balanced, multi-dimensional metrics. Build in course correction mechanisms: maturity targets may need adjustment based on organizational context changes, market shifts, or realized costs that differ from projections.

competencies.name: Analysis
competencies.description: The ability to understand opportunities, stakeholder needs, and system behavior through systematic investigation and data interpretation. In the IDP context, Analysis encompasses developer experience data analysis (DXI, NPS, SPACE), cognitive load assessment, DORA metric interpretation, CNCF maturity model evaluation, platform adoption analytics, and build-versus-buy decision analysis for platform capabilities.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands basic developer experience concepts and can parse developer survey feedback. Can identify common developer pain points from survey data. Familiar with the three DevEx dimensions (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state) and can categorize observed pain points.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can map developer friction points to existing platform capabilities and identify basic cognitive load sources. Can deploy standard developer experience surveys (DXI or equivalent) and interpret results. Can read DORA metric dashboards and identify delivery performance trends.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently translate complex stakeholder friction points into actionable platform requirements. Maps cognitive load bottlenecks to platform architectural requirements. Can conduct CNCF maturity model assessments and build-versus-buy analyses. Defines the Thinnest Viable Platform boundary based on data-driven prioritization.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can analyze shifting enterprise domains to identify new cognitive load sources, platform capability gaps, and strategic opportunities. Correlates developer experience metrics with business outcomes. Conducts competitive analysis against shadow IT alternatives and industry benchmarks.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Pioneers new analytical methods for developer experience measurement, cognitive load quantification, or platform value assessment that advance industry understanding beyond current frameworks.

competencies.name: Engineering
competencies.description: The ability to design, build, test, and implement technical solutions across infrastructure, software, and platform systems. In the IDP context, Engineering extends to cloud-native infrastructure (Kubernetes, service mesh), control plane architecture, workload specification design, infrastructure abstraction, golden path template engineering, and developer portal development.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands fundamental cloud infrastructure concepts, container basics, and basic CI/CD pipeline structure. Can follow existing golden path templates to deploy standard workloads.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can implement basic infrastructure components using Infrastructure-as-Code, build simple golden path templates, and configure standard CI/CD pipeline stages. Can extend existing platform capabilities following established patterns.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently design distributed platform components, author declarative configuration templates, build golden path templates with CI/CD, security, and observability integration, and develop developer portal extensions. Implements infrastructure abstractions that hide cloud provider complexity.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can architect complex, multi-tenant platform foundations with control plane patterns, continuous reconciliation, and multi-cloud portability. Resolves systemic integration challenges across architectural planes. Designs platform APIs that scale across hundreds of engineering teams.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops entirely new platform engineering paradigms, contributes to open-source platform tooling, or creates novel infrastructure abstraction patterns that redefine how organizations deliver internal developer services.

competencies.name: Leadership
competencies.description: The ability to inspire, guide, and motivate individuals and teams toward achieving platform-related goals and organizational transformation. In the IDP context, Leadership encompasses platform-as-product evangelism, developer-as-customer advocacy, cognitive load awareness leadership, cultural transformation through the DORA J-Curve, and community building.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Can participate effectively in platform team environments and support platform goals. Understands the developer-as-customer paradigm and can articulate why it matters.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can guide small platform engineering squads, foster adherence to agreed-upon ways of working, and facilitate team retrospectives focused on developer experience improvement.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can inspire platform teams to embrace DevOps culture, champion blameless post-mortems, establish psychological safety, and advocate for cognitive load reduction as a design constraint. Leads enabling team engagements with consuming teams.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can lead large-scale cultural transformations from project-based infrastructure to product-oriented platform engineering. Navigates the J-Curve, sustains executive sponsorship through challenges, and manages organizational resistance. Builds and leads developer champion communities.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Acts as an industry-recognized visionary, shaping the discourse on platform engineering culture, developer experience, and organizational design for platform teams. Contributes to industry conferences, publications, and standards bodies.

competencies.name: Management
competencies.description: The ability to plan, organize, coordinate, and control resources, activities, and work execution toward defined objectives. In the IDP context, Management extends to product-centric delivery management, platform team scaling, cross-functional coordination, FinOps program management, and adoption program management.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands basic task tracking and team coordination. Can use standard project management tools to track platform work items.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can manage the delivery of discrete platform capabilities, organize sprint cadence, and coordinate daily operational workflows. Tracks platform adoption metrics and reports progress.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently orchestrate cross-functional platform delivery cycles, balance technical debt against capability velocity, manage platform SLOs, and coordinate FinOps programs. Implements product-centric work management practices.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can adapt delivery structures across highly matrixed environments, transition organizations from project-based to product-centric funding, manage multi-team platform organizations, and coordinate vendor partnerships for platform components.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops novel management and operational frameworks that redefine how enterprises deliver internal developer platform services. Creates new approaches to platform team scaling, cross-organizational coordination, or FinOps governance.

competencies.name: Platform Security And Compliance Enforcement
competencies.description: The ability to design, implement, automate, and enforce security policies and compliance requirements across platform systems and consuming workloads. In the IDP context, this competency is enriched with SLSA framework implementation, software supply chain security, policy-as-code authoring, AI-generated code risk management, and guardrail-versus-gate design philosophy.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands basic security principles, compliance requirements, and the concept of policy-as-code. Can identify common security risks in platform configurations. Familiar with the SLSA framework levels.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can configure basic security settings, implement access controls based on documented procedures, and deploy standard security scanning tools in CI pipelines. Can author simple policy-as-code rules for common security requirements.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently design comprehensive security architectures embedding security into golden paths, implement SLSA Level 2 supply chain security, author complex policy-as-code (OPA/Rego), configure admission controllers, and automate compliance auditing.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can adapt security strategies to address novel threats (AI-generated code vulnerabilities, supply chain attacks), architect zero-trust implementations across multi-cloud environments, and design adaptive security posture management that responds to emerging threat intelligence.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops new paradigms for platform security, pioneers novel supply chain security approaches, or advances the industry's understanding of security-as-enablement in platform engineering contexts.

competencies.name: Platform Strategic Alignment
competencies.description: The ability to align platform capabilities, investments, and evolution with business goals, enterprise architecture, and strategic direction. In the IDP context, this competency extends to developer productivity value modeling, CNCF maturity model application, TVP principle enforcement, platform competitive positioning, and strategic technology alignment (particularly AI enablement).

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands the high-level business drivers for the IDP investment. Can articulate the basic value proposition of platform engineering in business terms.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can articulate how specific platform capabilities support identified business opportunities. Can apply the CNCF maturity model to assess current state and communicate results. Understands the TVP principle.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can develop and manage platform roadmaps that demonstrably drive business value and ROI. Applies TVP discipline to scope decisions. Demonstrates platform value through multi-dimensional metrics and business language reporting.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can pivot platform strategy in response to shifting market conditions, technology landscape changes, or organizational restructuring. Positions the platform as an AI enablement layer and strategic competitive asset. Conducts industry benchmarking and competitive analysis.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Pioneers new platform business models, creates novel approaches to internal product valuation, or advances the industry's understanding of how platform engineering drives enterprise competitive advantage.

competencies.name: Site Reliability
competencies.description: The ability to apply software engineering principles to operational problems, ensuring platform reliability, availability, and performance through systematic practices. In the IDP context, Site Reliability extends to platform SLO design for developer-facing services, developer productivity observability, feedback loop optimization, continuous reconciliation operations, and operational toil engineering.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands the concepts of SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, and basic incident response. Can follow documented incident response procedures and participate in post-mortems.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can participate in incident response, implement basic monitoring alerts for platform services, and track operational toil. Can define simple SLOs for platform services (availability, latency).

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently design robust monitoring systems for developer-facing platform services, define effective SLOs (provisioning time, build time, deployment success rate, portal availability), lead complex incident resolutions, and systematically reduce operational toil below the 50% cap.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can architect highly resilient, self-healing platform systems with continuous reconciliation, implement chaos engineering for platform resilience, and establish enterprise-wide SRE practices for internal developer services. Designs observability infrastructure that surfaces developer workflow bottlenecks.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops novel approaches to platform reliability engineering, developer productivity observability, or predictive reliability modeling that advance the application of SRE principles to internal developer platform contexts.

competencies.name: Stakeholder Representation
competencies.description: The ability to gather, synthesize, and advocate for stakeholder needs across diverse groups with competing priorities. In the IDP context, Stakeholder Representation extends to developer-as-customer advocacy, multi-persona needs synthesis, community engagement, and ecosystem advocacy.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands the different developer personas utilizing the platform (application developers, platform engineers, engineering managers, security officers, budget owners). Can identify basic stakeholder concerns.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can effectively gather and advocate for the needs of specific developer teams. Conducts developer feedback sessions and represents findings to the platform team. Maintains feedback channels.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can accurately balance competing requirements from developers (simplicity), security (compliance), engineering managers (velocity), and budget owners (ROI) to ensure the platform interface remains frictionless and stakeholder needs are addressed. Manages developer champion programs.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can navigate complex organizational politics, aligning executive objectives with developer operational realities. Maintains ongoing sponsorship through value demonstration. Manages resistance from teams whose workflows are disrupted by platform adoption. Builds inner-source communities.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Creates novel enterprise feedback loops, developer community models, or stakeholder representation approaches that radically improve platform evolution through democratized input. Represents organizational needs in industry standards bodies.

competencies.name: Product Management
competencies.description: The ability to apply product management discipline to internal platform development, encompassing user research, roadmap prioritization, competitive analysis (against shadow IT), adoption tracking, value demonstration, and the fundamental shift from project-based delivery to product-oriented platform evolution.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands the difference between project-based infrastructure delivery and product-oriented platform management. Can articulate why treating developers as customers changes the platform development approach. Familiar with the Thinnest Viable Platform concept.

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can maintain a platform product backlog, gather developer feedback through surveys and interviews, prioritize features based on developer impact, and track basic adoption metrics (monthly active users, feature usage). Applies Jobs-to-be-Done frameworks to understand developer motivations.

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently manage a platform product roadmap, conduct structured user research programs, apply TVP principles to scope decisions, demonstrate platform value through adoption and satisfaction metrics, and compete with shadow IT alternatives. Continuously validates that the platform deserves to exist through evidence of value delivery.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can transform organizational funding models from project-based to product-centric. Builds executive sponsorship by translating developer productivity improvements into business language. Establishes internal marketplace ecosystems where consuming teams contribute capabilities. Positions the platform as a strategic asset.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Develops novel platform product management models, creates new approaches to internal product valuation, or advances the industry's understanding of platform-as-product practices. Redefines how enterprises deliver internal developer services.

competencies.name: Developer Experience Design
competencies.description: The ability to research, measure, design, and continuously optimize the holistic experience of developers interacting with platform capabilities, encompassing the three DevEx dimensions (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state), developer satisfaction measurement, golden path design, and evidence-based platform improvement.

levels.name: Basic
levels.description: Understands the concept of developer experience as distinct from developer tooling. Can identify common developer pain points through informal observation. Familiar with the three DevEx dimensions (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state).

levels.name: Applies
levels.description: Can design and deploy developer experience surveys using validated instruments (DXI or equivalent). Conducts developer interviews and journey mapping exercises. Analyzes feedback data to identify improvement opportunities. Measures basic feedback loop durations (build time, pipeline time, provisioning time).

levels.name: Masters
levels.description: Can independently design and implement comprehensive developer experience measurement programs spanning individual, team, and system levels. Translates findings into actionable platform improvements with measurable impact. Establishes DXI and NPS tracking. Applies SPACE framework and DX Core 4 metrics. Designs golden path experiences that minimize cognitive load.

levels.name: Adapts
levels.description: Can establish organization-wide developer experience programs. Benchmarks against industry standards and demonstrates correlations between developer experience metrics and business outcomes (each DXI point improvement saves approximately 13 minutes per developer per week). Designs A/B testing frameworks for platform experience improvements.

levels.name: Innovating
levels.description: Pioneers new approaches to developer experience measurement, design, and optimization that advance industry understanding. Contributes to academic research or industry frameworks for developer experience. Creates novel cognitive load assessment methodologies for platform engineering contexts.

alphas.name: Opportunity
alphas.description: The foundational business drivers and strategic imperatives that justify investment in an internal developer platform, including developer productivity gaps, competitive pressure, AI enablement needs, and digital transformation requirements. In the IDP context, opportunity assessment draws on industry data from the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model, DORA State of DevOps Reports, and Forrester Total Economic Impact studies to quantify the business case for platform engineering.

states.name: Initiated
states.description: The organization recognizes that developer productivity challenges, infrastructure bottlenecks, or competitive pressures create a need for a dedicated internal developer platform. Initial champions begin advocating for a platform engineering approach.

checklist.name: Developer productivity pain points acknowledged
checklist.description: Developer productivity challenges (infrastructure friction, manual provisioning, duplicated effort across teams) are formally acknowledged at the engineering leadership level, moving beyond anecdotal complaints to recognized organizational concerns.

checklist.name: Infrastructure bottlenecks documented
checklist.description: Initial observations of infrastructure bottlenecks, configuration drift, or duplicated effort across development teams are documented with specific examples and rough quantification of impact.

checklist.name: Platform champion identified
checklist.description: At least one technical leader or engineering manager actively advocates for a platform engineering approach, articulating the distinction between an internal developer platform and traditional shared infrastructure services.

checklist.name: Industry context established
checklist.description: The discussion references relevant industry context: CNCF platform engineering adoption trends (55% of organizations report using some form of platform engineering), Gartner's projection (80% of software engineering organizations will establish platform teams by 2026), and DORA's characterization of platform engineering as a sociotechnical discipline.

states.name: Determined
states.description: The scope and parameters of the IDP opportunity are quantified through developer experience data, cognitive load assessment, and industry benchmarking against established frameworks such as the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model and DORA metrics.

checklist.name: Developer experience baseline established
checklist.description: Developer experience research quantifies the scope of productivity loss. Extraneous cognitive load percentage is estimated (target baseline: approximately 45% of total cognitive load spent on non-value-adding infrastructure tasks). Time spent on infrastructure provisioning, configuration, and waiting is measured per developer.

checklist.name: Industry benchmarking completed
checklist.description: Organizational maturity is assessed against industry benchmarks using the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model (four levels across five aspects: Investment, Adoption, Interfaces, Operations, Measurement) and DORA delivery performance metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, recovery time, rework rate).

checklist.name: Target developer population scoped
checklist.description: The target developer population and scope of initial platform coverage are identified. Candidate capability domains (from the CNCF's 13 platform capability domains or equivalent) are prioritized by developer impact. The Thinnest Viable Platform principle guides initial scope definition: "the smallest set of APIs, documentation, and tools needed to accelerate teams."

checklist.name: Competitive landscape assessed
checklist.description: Existing internal alternatives (shadow IT, team-maintained infrastructure, manual processes) are catalogued. The opportunity cost of the current state is quantified in terms of developer time, infrastructure cost, security risk, and delivery velocity.

states.name: Value Established
states.description: The IDP's value proposition is accepted by executive sponsors with a clear link to business outcomes across developer productivity, delivery performance, risk reduction, and strategic enablement.

checklist.name: Business case articulated
checklist.description: A formal business case connects platform investment to measurable outcomes: time-to-market acceleration (Forrester: 77% of organizations report shortened time to market), developer retention improvement (81% report positive retention impact), compliance cost reduction (83% report improved compliance), and strategic enablement (platform quality amplifies AI adoption impact per DORA 2025).

checklist.name: Executive sponsorship secured
checklist.description: Executive sponsors formally endorse the platform initiative with commitment to sustained investment. Sponsorship spans engineering leadership, security governance, and financial oversight.

checklist.name: Value proposition validated
checklist.description: The value proposition addresses both direct savings (infrastructure cost reduction, developer time reclamation) and strategic enablement (AI adoption readiness, competitive velocity, risk reduction). Stakeholders across all three focuses validate the opportunity.

checklist.name: Strategic alignment confirmed
checklist.description: The platform initiative is aligned with broader organizational strategy: digital transformation goals, technology modernization, talent retention priorities, and competitive positioning.

states.name: Viable
states.description: The platform business case demonstrates a viable economic return with quantified investment requirements, expected returns, risk factors, and payback timeline.

checklist.name: ROI model validated
checklist.description: ROI model calculates expected returns using industry-validated methodologies. The capacity reclamation calculation is grounded in measured data: developers affected multiplied by time saved multiplied by fully-loaded hourly cost. Reference benchmark: 300 engineers saving 45 minutes per day yields approximately 180 hours per engineer per year in reclaimed capacity.

checklist.name: Total cost of ownership documented
checklist.description: Total Cost of Ownership includes platform team personnel (the dominant cost), infrastructure and tooling, organizational change management, enabling team investment, and ongoing operational overhead. Industry reference: dedicated platform teams typically require 2-3 people at 50-100 developers, scaling to full dedicated teams at 100+ developers.

checklist.name: Financial projections approved
checklist.description: Payback period and Net Present Value are calculated and approved by financial stakeholders. Reference benchmark: Forrester TEI studies document ROI of 224% with 6-month payback period for mature IDP implementations.

checklist.name: Risk mitigation planned
checklist.description: Risk factors are documented and mitigation strategies are defined: adoption risk (the DORA J-Curve phenomenon), organizational resistance, technical complexity, shadow IT competition, and ongoing funding sustainability.

states.name: Addressed
states.description: The opportunity is actively being addressed by the operational internal developer platform, with measurable progress toward the defined value targets.

checklist.name: Platform operational
checklist.description: The IDP is operational and serving development teams with self-service capabilities, golden paths, and automated governance.

checklist.name: Delivery performance improving
checklist.description: DORA metrics demonstrate measurable improvement over the pre-platform baseline: lead time for changes, deployment frequency, change failure rate, failed deployment recovery time, and rework rate.

checklist.name: Adoption tracking to targets
checklist.description: Developer adoption rate tracks toward organizational targets. Elite-performing organizations target 80%+ adoption within six months. Adoption measurement includes both usage metrics and voluntary preference (developers choosing the platform over alternatives).

checklist.name: Value communication active
checklist.description: Value delivery is regularly communicated to sponsors in business language: dollars saved, developer hours reclaimed, time-to-market acceleration, security incidents prevented, compliance cost avoided.

states.name: Benefit Accrued
states.description: The expected benefits of the IDP investment are consistently realized and the platform delivers compounding returns that justify sustained and growing investment.

checklist.name: ROI targets met or exceeded
checklist.description: Platform ROI meets or exceeds initial projections. Multi-year tracking demonstrates sustained returns. Reference: organizations at mature platform adoption levels report 30-40% lower infrastructure costs per developer.

checklist.name: Productivity improvements sustained
checklist.description: Developer productivity improvements are sustained and growing over time. The DORA J-Curve has been traversed: initial gains, temporary complexity dip, and recovery at higher performance levels are documented.

checklist.name: Strategic value demonstrated
checklist.description: The platform amplifies the impact of other technology investments, particularly AI adoption. Per DORA 2025: "when platform quality is high, the effect of AI adoption on organizational performance becomes strong and positive." Platform benefits compound as adoption, capabilities, and organizational maturity grow.

checklist.name: Competitive advantage recognized
checklist.description: Organizational competitive advantage from the platform is recognized internally and by industry peers. The platform is positioned as a strategic asset rather than a cost center.

narratives.name: Opportunity Narrative
narratives.description: The journey of recognizing, quantifying, and realizing the business opportunity for an internal developer platform.

narrativeContexts.context: The organization operates without a unified internal developer platform. Development teams independently manage their own infrastructure, creating duplicated effort, inconsistent practices, and mounting cognitive load. Each team makes independent technology choices, leading to configuration drift, security gaps, and infrastructure sprawl. Developers spend approximately 45% of their cognitive capacity on extraneous tasks -- provisioning, configuration, debugging infrastructure issues -- rather than building features that deliver business value.

A convergence of pressures creates an undeniable case for change: competitive organizations deliver features faster through platform engineering, developer retention suffers as engineers leave for organizations with better developer experience, AI adoption requires a governed platform for safe distribution of AI-generated changes, and industry data (CNCF, DORA, Gartner) validates that platform engineering has moved from experimental to mainstream practice.

The organization commits to building an internal developer platform. The journey involves quantifying the opportunity through developer experience research and industry benchmarking, securing executive sponsorship through a compelling business case, defining the Thinnest Viable Platform scope, and navigating the inevitable DORA J-Curve where initial enthusiasm meets implementation complexity before performance recovers at higher levels.

The organization operates with a mature internal developer platform that delivers compounding returns. Developer productivity has measurably improved, delivery performance meets elite benchmarks, the platform amplifies AI adoption impact, and the organization has established platform engineering as a recognized competitive advantage.

alphas.name: Stakeholders
alphas.description: The individuals, groups, and organizational roles affected by or influencing the internal developer platform, encompassing platform producers (platform engineers), platform consumers (application developers), executive sponsors, security governance officers, and financial oversight. In the IDP context, the stakeholder landscape is characterized by the developer-as-customer paradigm, where application developers are treated as primary customers whose experience determines platform success.

states.name: Recognized
states.description: Key IDP stakeholder groups are identified across producer, consumer, governance, and sponsorship roles. The developer-as-customer paradigm is understood as the foundational stakeholder engagement principle.

checklist.name: Primary stakeholder groups documented
checklist.description: The five primary IDP stakeholder groups are formally documented: application developers (consumers), platform engineers (producers), engineering managers (team leaders), security and compliance officers (governance), and budget owners (financial oversight). Each group's needs, motivations, and potential resistance patterns are characterized.

checklist.name: Developer-as-customer paradigm understood
checklist.description: The organization understands that developers are not passive recipients of infrastructure but active customers whose experience determines platform success. The platform team treats developers with the same product management rigor applied to external customers.

checklist.name: Stakeholder influence mapped
checklist.description: Stakeholder influence and impact on platform success are assessed. Power/interest mapping or equivalent stakeholder analysis identifies which groups have the most influence over platform adoption and which are most affected by platform decisions.

checklist.name: Resistance patterns anticipated
checklist.description: Potential resistance patterns are anticipated: developers skeptical due to previous failed "platform" initiatives, infrastructure teams concerned about role changes, security teams wary of reduced control, and managers uncertain about organizational topology changes.

states.name: Represented
states.description: Stakeholder representatives are designated with formal feedback channels established. Platform product management synthesizes all stakeholder needs into a coherent platform vision.

checklist.name: Developer advocates designated
checklist.description: Developer advocates or champions represent application developer interests. These are developers within consuming teams who have direct experience with the platform and can articulate consumer needs authentically.

checklist.name: Platform product management established
checklist.description: A platform product management function (person or role) represents the synthesis of all stakeholder needs. This role conducts user research, prioritizes the platform roadmap, and maintains the balance between competing stakeholder interests.

checklist.name: Governance stakeholder channels active
checklist.description: Security and compliance stakeholders have formal input channels to platform decisions. These channels are collaborative (security contributes to governance model design) rather than adversarial (security imposes requirements after the fact).

checklist.name: Budget owners engaged
checklist.description: Budget owners have visibility into platform investment levels, value delivery metrics, and cost attribution. Financial governance is integrated into the platform operating model rather than operating as an external control.

states.name: Involved
states.description: Stakeholders actively participate in platform direction through structured engagement mechanisms including developer experience surveys, user research, security collaboration, and value reporting.

checklist.name: Developer experience measurement active
checklist.description: Regular developer experience surveys capture consumer sentiment using validated instruments (Developer Experience Index, Net Promoter Score). Measurement cadence is established (quarterly minimum) with results shared transparently.

checklist.name: User research methods deployed
checklist.description: Qualitative user research methods (developer interviews, journey mapping, observational studies, day-in-the-life analysis) engage developers directly. Research findings inform platform roadmap priorities.

checklist.name: Security collaboration established
checklist.description: Security stakeholders collaborate on governance model design rather than imposing requirements post-hoc. The guardrails-versus-gates philosophy is jointly developed and agreed upon.

checklist.name: Value reporting active
checklist.description: Budget owners and engineering managers receive regular value reports demonstrating platform ROI: developer time saved, delivery performance improvement, cost optimization achieved, and security posture improvement.

checklist.name: Feedback loops operational
checklist.description: Structured feedback loops connect stakeholder input to platform improvement: developer surveys drive roadmap changes, incident post-mortems improve operational practices, and adoption analytics identify capability gaps.

states.name: In Agreement
states.description: Stakeholder expectations are aligned around platform capabilities, priorities, governance model, and investment level. Competing interests are resolved through transparent prioritization.

checklist.name: Platform roadmap reflects balanced input
checklist.description: The platform roadmap demonstrably reflects input from all stakeholder groups. Prioritization criteria are transparent (developer impact, strategic alignment, security requirements, cost efficiency), and trade-offs between competing interests are explicitly documented.

checklist.name: Governance model agreed
checklist.description: The governance model (guardrails versus gates, policy-as-code versus manual review, golden path compliance versus enforcement) is agreed upon by security and development stakeholders. The target state for manual gates (5-10% of changes) is accepted.

checklist.name: Funding model aligned
checklist.description: Budget allocation reflects product-centric rather than project-based funding. The platform has sustained, centrally allocated budget rather than annual project approval cycles.

checklist.name: Service level expectations documented
checklist.description: Service level expectations between the platform team and consuming teams are documented, including platform availability SLOs, provisioning time targets, and support response expectations.

states.name: Satisfied for Deployment
states.description: Stakeholders approve the platform for organizational deployment based on demonstrated capability with early adopter teams.

checklist.name: Early adopter validation positive
checklist.description: Early adopter teams validate platform capabilities and provide positive feedback. Time to First Deploy targets are met (target: one day for new developers). Golden path adoption rates among early adopters demonstrate voluntary preference.

checklist.name: Security stakeholders confirm governance
checklist.description: Security and compliance stakeholders confirm that governance requirements are met through automated policy enforcement, supply chain security controls, and audit trail completeness.

checklist.name: Leadership endorses broader adoption
checklist.description: Engineering leadership endorses platform adoption across the organization. The endorsement is based on demonstrated value with early adopters, not mandate. The platform is positioned as compelling and optional, not mandatory.

checklist.name: Enabling team support prepared
checklist.description: Enabling team support plan is in place for broader adoption. Teams are trained to facilitate platform onboarding through temporary coaching engagements ("teaching how to fish"), with explicit transition plans from Collaboration to X-as-a-Service interaction modes.

states.name: Satisfied in Use
states.description: Stakeholders are satisfied with the operational platform and its ongoing evolution. The platform is recognized as a valued organizational asset by all stakeholder groups.

checklist.name: Developer satisfaction targets met
checklist.description: Developer satisfaction metrics meet or exceed organizational targets. Elite-performing platforms target NPS greater than +40. Developer Experience Index scores demonstrate sustained improvement over baseline.

checklist.name: Platform team satisfaction healthy
checklist.description: Platform team satisfaction with their operating model is healthy. Platform engineers report meaningful work, manageable operational toil (below 50% per SRE principles), and career growth opportunities.

checklist.name: Governance effectiveness confirmed
checklist.description: Security and compliance stakeholders confirm continuous governance effectiveness. Automated policy enforcement covers the vast majority of changes, with manual gates reserved for genuinely exceptional cases.

checklist.name: ROI sustained
checklist.description: Budget owners observe sustained or growing ROI from platform investment. Cost per developer trends favorably. Infrastructure efficiency improves with platform maturity.

checklist.name: Community contribution active
checklist.description: Community contribution patterns indicate deep stakeholder investment in the platform ecosystem. Consuming teams contribute golden path templates, documentation improvements, and capability extensions through inner-source practices. Shadow IT decreases as developers voluntarily prefer platform-provided capabilities.

narratives.name: Stakeholders Narrative
narratives.description: The stakeholder journey from recognition through satisfaction, positioning the developer as hero and platform team as guide.

narrativeContexts.narrativeElementName: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeContexts.context: The application developer (Hero) faces daily frustration: provisioning a new service requires filing tickets and waiting days, every team has different infrastructure configurations leading to inconsistent deployments, debugging production issues requires understanding platform internals that are outside their expertise, and security reviews add weeks to release timelines. The cognitive load of infrastructure management prevents the developer from focusing on the domain problems they were hired to solve.

narrativeContexts.narrativeElementName: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeContexts.context: The platform engineering team (Guide) offers a clear plan: a developer portal where all platform capabilities are discoverable and self-service, golden paths that make the right way the easy path, guardrails that embed security without requiring manual gates, and enabling teams that coach new consumers through adoption. The plan follows the Thinnest Viable Platform principle -- starting with the most impactful capabilities and expanding based on demonstrated developer need.

narrativeContexts.narrativeElementName: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeContexts.context: The developer adopts the platform voluntarily -- not because it is mandated but because it demonstrably reduces their cognitive load and accelerates their delivery. Within a day, a new developer deploys their first application through a golden path. Within a month, they cannot imagine working without the platform. Their satisfaction score rises, their delivery velocity increases, and they begin contributing golden path improvements back to the platform ecosystem.

alphas.name: Platform Value And Economics
alphas.description: The financial and outcome-based justification, measurement, and optimization of internal developer platform investment, encompassing developer time savings, infrastructure cost management, developer retention economics, and the strategic value multiplier effect of platform quality. In the IDP context, economics measurement draws on DORA metrics, the DX Core 4 framework, Forrester Total Economic Impact methodologies, and the SPACE framework to provide multi-dimensional value quantification that guards against Goodhart's Law.

states.name: Modeled
states.description: Financial needs and potential productivity returns from IDP investment are identified and initially quantified using industry-validated methodologies and organizational baseline data.

checklist.name: Developer time baseline established
checklist.description: Developer time spent on extraneous tasks (infrastructure provisioning, configuration management, waiting for approvals, debugging infrastructure issues) is estimated through developer experience surveys, time studies, and workflow analysis. Reference benchmark: typical pre-platform extraneous cognitive load is approximately 45% of total developer effort.

checklist.name: Infrastructure cost baseline documented
checklist.description: Current infrastructure cost per developer is calculated. Total infrastructure spending is attributed to teams where possible. Cloud spend, tooling licenses, and operational overhead are inventoried.

checklist.name: Retention economics estimated
checklist.description: Developer retention costs and platform impact on retention are estimated. Reference: preventing five senior engineers from leaving avoids approximately one to two million dollars in replacement and ramp-up costs. Industry data indicates 81% of organizations report that developer experience investment positively impacts recruitment and retention.

checklist.name: ROI model created
checklist.description: An initial ROI model is created using the capacity reclamation formula: developers affected multiplied by time saved multiplied by fully-loaded hourly cost. Industry reference benchmark: 300 engineers saving 45 minutes per day at $150/hour yields approximately $8.1 million in reclaimed capacity per year.

checklist.name: Industry benchmarks referenced
checklist.description: Industry benchmarks for IDP ROI are referenced, including Forrester Total Economic Impact studies (documented ROI of 224% with 6-month payback) and DORA performance benchmarks for elite-performing organizations.

states.name: Allocated
states.description: Platform investment budgets are formally allocated based on the modeled financial case, with cost categories, funding models, and initial spending targets established.

checklist.name: Budget formally allocated
checklist.description: Dedicated platform budget is formally allocated and centrally funded. The platform investment is treated as product investment with sustained funding, not as a time-bounded project budget.

checklist.name: Cost categories defined
checklist.description: Cost categories are defined: platform team personnel (typically the dominant cost), infrastructure and cloud services, tooling and licensing, organizational change and enablement, and ongoing operational overhead.

checklist.name: Funding model selected
checklist.description: The funding model is selected: centralized funding for core platform capabilities, with cost attribution (chargeback or showback) models for infrastructure consumption by consuming teams.

checklist.name: Investment phasing planned
checklist.description: Investment is phased to align with maturity progression: initial investment in the Thinnest Viable Platform, followed by incremental investment driven by demonstrated value and measured developer need.

states.name: Measured
states.description: Platform value is systematically tracked through multi-dimensional metrics combining developer productivity, delivery performance, infrastructure cost, and developer satisfaction data.

checklist.name: DORA metrics collected
checklist.description: DORA metrics are collected and reported: lead time for changes, deployment frequency, change failure rate, failed deployment recovery time, and rework rate (the fifth metric added in 2024). Measurement compares pre-platform and post-platform baselines.

checklist.name: Developer experience metrics tracked
checklist.description: Developer experience metrics are tracked using validated instruments: Developer Experience Index (DXI), Net Promoter Score (NPS), and satisfaction surveys. The three DevEx dimensions (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state) are measured at individual, team, and system levels.

checklist.name: DX Core 4 framework implemented
checklist.description: The DX Core 4 framework is implemented to operationalize developer experience measurement through four metrics: Speed (diffs per engineer at team level), Effectiveness (DXI from 14 survey items), Quality (change failure rate), and Impact (percentage of time on new capabilities versus maintenance).

checklist.name: Cost attribution operational
checklist.description: Cost attribution models (chargeback or showback) assign platform infrastructure costs to consuming teams. Infrastructure cost per developer is calculated and benchmarked against industry and historical baselines.

checklist.name: Goodhart's Law mitigated
checklist.description: Multi-dimensional measurement mitigates Goodhart's Law ("when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"). No single metric is used as the sole platform success indicator. The SPACE framework's five dimensions (Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, Efficiency) inform balanced measurement design.

states.name: Optimized
states.description: Platform economics are actively managed with continuous cost optimization, demonstrated ROI, and product-centric investment governance.

checklist.name: FinOps practices operational
checklist.description: FinOps practices continuously optimize infrastructure spending: right-sizing compute resources, leveraging reserved capacity, automating cleanup of idle resources, and identifying cost anomalies. Infrastructure cost per developer trends downward as platform maturity increases.

checklist.name: ROI regularly communicated
checklist.description: Platform ROI is regularly calculated and communicated to leadership in business language. Value reports translate developer productivity improvements into financial terms that executive stakeholders understand and value.

checklist.name: Value metrics linked to business outcomes
checklist.description: Value metrics explicitly link platform investment to business outcomes: time-to-market acceleration, revenue impact of faster feature delivery, risk reduction from automated governance, and talent retention value of superior developer experience.

checklist.name: Product-centric funding established
checklist.description: Product-centric funding replaces project-based budgets for platform investment. The platform is evaluated as internal product investment comparable to external-facing products, with ongoing funding justified by continuous value delivery rather than one-time project approval.

states.name: Value-Driven
states.description: Platform investment decisions are driven by demonstrated value creation. The platform is recognized as a strategic asset and force multiplier that amplifies the impact of all other technology investments.

checklist.name: Platform quality amplifies organizational performance
checklist.description: Platform quality directly enables organizational performance improvements. Per DORA 2025: "when platform quality is high, the effect of AI adoption on organizational performance becomes strong and positive." The platform is positioned as an AI enablement layer.

checklist.name: Compounding returns demonstrated
checklist.description: The platform demonstrates compounding returns on investment over multiple years. Each additional capability, golden path, and abstraction increases the value delivered per developer without proportional cost increase.

checklist.name: Strategic asset recognition
checklist.description: The platform is recognized as a competitive differentiator by organizational leadership. Investment decisions treat the platform as strategic infrastructure comparable to customer-facing platforms in terms of quality expectations and investment priority.

checklist.name: Opportunity cost models complete
checklist.description: Financial models capture both direct savings (infrastructure cost reduction, developer time reclamation) and opportunity cost avoidance (developers freed for feature development, faster time-to-market, reduced security incident costs).

narratives.name: Platform Value And Economics Narrative
narratives.description: The economic journey from initial modeling through strategic value recognition for IDP investment.

narrativeContexts.context: An enterprise with 300 software engineers spends an estimated $8.1 million per year in developer capacity on infrastructure tasks: provisioning environments, debugging configuration issues, waiting for manual approvals, and maintaining team-specific tooling. Infrastructure costs are opaque, with no clear attribution to consuming teams. Developer retention is declining, with exit interviews citing infrastructure friction as a contributing factor. Shadow IT proliferates as teams build their own automation to work around central constraints.

Quantify the economic case for an internal developer platform, establish multi-dimensional measurement, implement FinOps practices, and demonstrate sustained ROI that justifies ongoing investment at the executive level.

A developer productivity economics program is established: baseline measurements are captured (DORA metrics, developer time studies, infrastructure cost analysis, retention data), an ROI model is built using Forrester TEI methodology, FinOps practices are implemented for continuous cost optimization, DX Core 4 metrics provide ongoing measurement, and quarterly value reports communicate returns in business language.

Platform ROI exceeds 200% within three years, with a payback period under 12 months. Developer time on extraneous tasks drops from 45% to 15% of total cognitive load. Infrastructure cost per developer decreases by 35%. Developer NPS increases from -10 to +45. The platform is recognized by the board as a strategic asset, securing sustained product-centric funding.

alphas.name: Platform Risk And Compliance
alphas.description: The comprehensive security architecture of the internal developer platform, embedding identity management, access control, software supply chain integrity, policy enforcement, and compliance automation into the platform as enablers rather than impediments to developer velocity. In the IDP context, security posture is built on the principle that the secure path should be the easy path: golden paths embed security by default, guardrails prevent insecure configurations, and policy-as-code replaces manual security review for the vast majority of changes.

states.name: Assessed
states.description: Security risks, compliance requirements, and threat landscape are systematically identified and assessed. The security team understands the current posture and the gap between the current state and the target state for platform security.

checklist.name: Security risk inventory completed
checklist.description: All security risks relevant to the platform are inventoried: identity and access management gaps, secrets management weaknesses, supply chain vulnerabilities, network security exposures, and compliance requirement coverage gaps.

checklist.name: Compliance requirements mapped
checklist.description: Regulatory and organizational compliance requirements are mapped to platform capabilities. Gaps between current compliance coverage and requirements are quantified. Industry frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST) inform the compliance mapping.

checklist.name: Threat model established
checklist.description: A threat model for the platform is established covering identity compromise, supply chain attacks, container escape, lateral movement, data exfiltration, and AI-generated code vulnerabilities. Gartner projects 30% of vulnerabilities from AI coding by 2027, with AI-generated code producing flaws at 2.74x the rate of human-written code.

checklist.name: Security responsibility model defined
checklist.description: Security responsibilities between the platform team and consuming teams are documented using a shared responsibility model. The platform is responsible for infrastructure security, golden path security integration, and policy enforcement; consuming teams are responsible for application-level security within the guardrails the platform provides.

states.name: Foundational
states.description: Core identity, access control, and secrets management are established as P0 security priorities. These foundational controls must be in place before advancing to shift-left practices.

checklist.name: SSO with MFA enforced
checklist.description: Workforce single sign-on with multi-factor authentication is enforced for all platform access. No shared credentials or local accounts exist for platform systems.

checklist.name: Unique service identities established
checklist.description: Unique service and CI identities replace shared credentials. Every automated process has its own identity with least-privilege access. Workload identity federation eliminates long-lived secrets where possible.

checklist.name: Centralized secrets management operational
checklist.description: Centralized secrets management architecture is operational with automated injection into workloads. Secrets are never stored in source code, environment variables, or configuration files. Secret rotation is automated for high-risk credentials.

checklist.name: Access control policies defined
checklist.description: Role-based access control policies are defined and enforced for platform resources. The principle of least privilege governs all access grants. Emergency access ("break glass") procedures are documented and audited.

states.name: Shift-Left
states.description: Security controls are embedded into development and delivery pipelines, moving security earlier in the software lifecycle. Golden paths make security the default, not an afterthought.

checklist.name: Branch protection enforced
checklist.description: Branch and workflow protection prevents unauthorized changes to critical paths. Code review requirements, status check requirements, and merge restrictions are enforced through platform automation.

checklist.name: Security scanning integrated
checklist.description: Dependency scanning (Software Composition Analysis), Static Application Security Testing (SAST), and container image scanning are integrated into CI pipelines as standard golden path stages. Security policy violations block pipeline progression with clear remediation guidance.

checklist.name: Golden paths embed security
checklist.description: Golden paths embed security requirements by default. A developer following a golden path automatically gets secure configurations, dependency scanning, container hardening, and compliance checks without additional effort. The secure path is the easy path.

checklist.name: Central audit logging active
checklist.description: Central audit logging captures all security-relevant events across platform systems and consumer workloads. Logs are immutable, searchable, and retained according to compliance requirements.

checklist.name: Security review scope defined
checklist.description: The scope of manual security review is explicitly defined: only novel architectures, high-risk changes, or exception requests require human security review. Standard changes following golden paths are approved through automated policy enforcement.

states.name: Automated Governance
states.description: Policy-as-code and supply chain security automate comprehensive governance with minimal manual intervention. The platform enforces security policies at build time, deployment time, and runtime through automated mechanisms.

checklist.name: SLSA Level 2 achieved
checklist.description: Build provenance and artifact signing meet SLSA Level 2: builds run on dedicated infrastructure with signed provenance documents that are tamper-proof and verifiable. Keyless artifact signing (tied to OIDC identity) eliminates key management burden.

checklist.name: Admission controllers enforcing
checklist.description: Admission controllers enforce security policies at deployment time: container security context requirements, resource limits, network policy requirements, and image provenance verification. Non-compliant workloads are prevented from reaching production.

checklist.name: Runtime policies operational
checklist.description: Runtime security policies constrain workload behavior in production: network segmentation, system call filtering, file system access restrictions, and privileged escalation prevention.

checklist.name: Manual gates minimized
checklist.description: Manual security gates are reduced to 5-10% of changes. Policy-as-code (using OPA/Rego for complex logic, YAML-based policies for simpler scenarios) handles the vast majority of security decisions automatically.

checklist.name: AI code scrutiny established
checklist.description: AI-generated code is subject to enhanced security scrutiny through additional scanning rules and review triggers, addressing the projected higher flaw rate in AI-generated code.

states.name: Adaptive Security
states.description: Security posture proactively adapts to emerging threats, evolving regulations, and new technology vectors. The platform's security model is resilient and self-improving.

checklist.name: Threat intelligence integrated
checklist.description: Threat intelligence feeds inform platform security policy updates. Known vulnerability databases, supply chain threat advisories, and industry security alerts trigger automatic policy adjustments where appropriate.

checklist.name: Zero-trust fully implemented
checklist.description: Zero-trust principles are fully implemented across all platform layers: verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, assume breach. Every request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted regardless of network location.

checklist.name: Regulatory agility demonstrated
checklist.description: New regulatory requirements are rapidly translated into automated policies. The time from regulatory requirement to automated enforcement is measured and continuously shortened.

checklist.name: Security posture validated continuously
checklist.description: Security posture is continuously validated through automated penetration testing, chaos engineering exercises, and red team operations. Validation results feed back into policy updates and security improvements.

narratives.name: Platform Risk And Compliance Narrative
narratives.description: The security maturity journey from fragmented practices to automated, adaptive governance.

narrativeContexts.context: Most organizations beginning their IDP security journey have fragmented security practices: shared credentials, manual security reviews that bottleneck delivery, inconsistent container scanning across teams, and limited supply chain security. Only 13.1% of organizations reach the Optimizing level of the CNCF maturity model's Operations aspect. The starting point is honest assessment of where security gaps exist without judgment.

The target is Automated Governance (Level 4) for most security aspects, with Adaptive Security (Level 5) reserved for high-risk domains. The investment rationale is clear: automated security reduces the cost of governance while increasing coverage. Manual gates should be reduced to 5-10% of changes, freeing security teams to focus on novel threats rather than routine reviews.

The journey progresses through identity foundations (P0), pipeline security integration (shift-left), and policy automation. Each phase requires investment in tooling (SLSA infrastructure, admission controllers, policy engines), people (security engineering skills on the platform team), and organizational change (security-as-enablement culture shift). The J-Curve applies to security: initial friction as new controls are introduced, followed by velocity improvement as automation replaces manual processes.

Security posture progress is tracked through metrics: percentage of changes requiring manual security review (target: below 10%), mean time to remediate vulnerabilities, SLSA level achieved, number of security incidents attributable to platform-governed code, and developer perception of security friction. Course correction mechanisms include quarterly security posture reviews and developer feedback on governance friction.

alphas.name: Requirements
alphas.description: The capabilities, features, and quality attributes the internal developer platform must satisfy, framed through the lens of developer cognitive load reduction, self-service enablement, feedback loop acceleration, and flow state optimization rather than traditional feature requirements. In the IDP context, requirements are gathered through structured developer experience research (DXI surveys, SPACE framework assessment, cognitive load measurement, feedback loop mapping) and prioritized by their impact on the three DevEx dimensions.

states.name: Conceived
states.description: Developer experience pain points and platform needs are identified through initial research and stakeholder engagement. The three DevEx dimensions (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state) frame the discovery process.

checklist.name: Developer pain points captured
checklist.description: Initial developer experience surveys or interviews capture the most significant pain points. Common friction categories are identified: slow provisioning, complex configuration, inconsistent tooling, security bottlenecks, and poor documentation.

checklist.name: Cognitive load sources categorized
checklist.description: Cognitive load sources are categorized using the Team Topologies framework: intrinsic (inherent domain complexity that should be preserved), extraneous (non-value-adding burden that should be eliminated), and germane (productive problem-solving that should be maximized). Baseline distribution is estimated for target developer populations.

checklist.name: Self-service gaps identified
checklist.description: Self-service gaps are identified: what requires tickets, manual processes, or platform team involvement today that developers should be able to do independently. Each gap is assessed for automation feasibility and developer impact.

checklist.name: Feedback loop durations measured
checklist.description: Feedback loop durations are measured for critical developer workflows: build time, test execution time, deployment time, environment provisioning time, and security review turnaround. These durations establish the baseline for improvement targeting.

checklist.name: Developer personas documented
checklist.description: Developer personas and their distinct needs are documented (application developers, data engineers, ML engineers, mobile developers). Each persona has different cognitive load profiles and self-service priorities.

states.name: Bounded
states.description: The scope of developer experience needs is defined with clear boundaries aligned to the Thinnest Viable Platform principle. Needs are prioritized by cognitive load impact and developer velocity improvement potential.

checklist.name: TVP boundary established
checklist.description: The Thinnest Viable Platform boundary is established: "the smallest set of APIs, documentation, and tools needed to accelerate teams." The TVP discipline prevents scope creep by requiring evidence of developer need before adding capabilities. "A TVP could be just a wiki page if that is all you need."

checklist.name: Needs prioritized by impact
checklist.description: Developer experience needs are prioritized by their impact on cognitive load reduction and developer velocity. High-impact, high-frequency pain points are addressed first.

checklist.name: Capability domains mapped
checklist.description: Candidate capability domains (from the CNCF's 13 platform capability domains) are mapped to identified needs. Build-versus-buy decisions are documented for each domain.

checklist.name: Platform-versus-team responsibilities defined
checklist.description: The scope explicitly distinguishes between platform-provided capabilities (standardized, self-service, governed) and team-owned responsibilities (application logic, domain-specific tooling, business rules).

states.name: Coherent
states.description: Developer experience needs are organized into a coherent framework with measurable acceptance criteria structured across the three DevEx dimensions.

checklist.name: Needs structured across DevEx dimensions
checklist.description: Needs are organized across the three DevEx dimensions: feedback loops (speed and quality of responses to developer actions), cognitive load (mental processing required to accomplish work), and flow state (ability to be fully absorbed in productive work).

checklist.name: Measurable acceptance criteria defined
checklist.description: Acceptance criteria use measurable targets: provisioning time under 30 minutes for standard capabilities, Time to First Deploy under one day for new developers, build time under 10 minutes for standard projects, deployment frequency at least daily for elite teams.

checklist.name: SPACE framework alignment
checklist.description: The SPACE framework dimensions (Satisfaction and well-being, Performance, Activity, Communication and collaboration, Efficiency and flow) inform need categorization, ensuring multi-dimensional coverage that avoids single-metric optimization.

checklist.name: Conflicting needs resolved
checklist.description: Conflicting needs between stakeholder groups are identified and resolved. Security requirements versus developer autonomy, standardization versus flexibility, and simplicity versus capability are balanced through explicit trade-off decisions.

states.name: Acceptable
states.description: All stakeholder groups agree that the defined needs reflect their requirements and the platform's value proposition. The scope is accepted as appropriate for the investment level.

checklist.name: Developer validation complete
checklist.description: Application developers validate that the needs address their most significant cognitive load sources. Validation uses developer feedback sessions, prototype demonstrations, or early access programs.

checklist.name: Security validation complete
checklist.description: Security stakeholders confirm that governance needs are adequately represented. The balance between automated governance and manual review is accepted.

checklist.name: Manager validation complete
checklist.description: Engineering managers validate that team-level productivity needs are captured. Impact on team velocity, cognitive load distribution, and delivery performance is confirmed.

checklist.name: Feasibility confirmed
checklist.description: Platform engineers confirm that the needs are technically feasible within the target architecture, timeline, and investment constraints. Implementation risks are identified and mitigated.

states.name: Addressed
states.description: The operational platform satisfies the defined developer experience needs with measurable evidence of improvement across all three DevEx dimensions.

checklist.name: DevEx metrics improving
checklist.description: Developer experience metrics demonstrate improvement against baseline measurements across all three dimensions. Feedback loop durations decrease, extraneous cognitive load percentage drops, and flow state indicators improve.

checklist.name: Self-service capabilities operational
