checklist.description: Self-service capabilities address the highest-priority provisioning and configuration needs. Developers can independently create projects, provision infrastructure, deploy to non-production environments, and access platform services without tickets or manual processes.

checklist.name: Feedback loop targets met
checklist.description: Feedback loop durations meet or exceed target thresholds: build time, test time, deployment time, and provisioning time are within defined targets.

checklist.name: Cognitive load targets progressing
checklist.description: Cognitive load assessment shows progress toward the target distribution: approximately 50% intrinsic (domain complexity), 15% extraneous (platform friction), and 35% germane (productive problem-solving).

checklist.name: Developer satisfaction targets met
checklist.description: Developer satisfaction (NPS) meets organizational targets. DXI scores demonstrate improvement. Each DXI point improvement saves approximately 13 minutes per developer per week.

states.name: Fulfilled
states.description: All developer experience needs are met and the platform continuously discovers and addresses emerging needs through product management discipline and ongoing research.

checklist.name: Comprehensive measurement achieved
checklist.description: Comprehensive developer experience measurement (DXI, DORA, SPACE, DX Core 4) demonstrates sustained excellence across all dimensions. Metrics are industry-leading.

checklist.name: Golden path coverage comprehensive
checklist.description: Golden paths cover the majority of developer workflows with high voluntary adoption (target: 80%+ adoption rate). Developers follow golden paths because they are genuinely the best way to work, not because they are mandated.

checklist.name: Proactive needs discovery
checklist.description: The platform proactively identifies emerging needs through continuous developer experience research and behavioral telemetry. New needs are discovered before they become pain points.

checklist.name: Continuous evolution
checklist.description: The platform evolves ahead of developer needs through product management discipline. The developer experience is recognized as a competitive advantage for talent retention and organizational velocity.

narratives.name: Requirements Narrative
narratives.description: The developer experience needs journey from initial pain point discovery through comprehensive fulfillment.

narrativeContexts.context: Application developers across the organization experience significant cognitive load from infrastructure complexity. Developer experience surveys reveal that 45% of developer time is spent on extraneous tasks: environment provisioning (average 3 days), security review turnaround (average 2 weeks), deployment troubleshooting (inconsistent across teams), and configuration management (tribal knowledge required). DORA metrics show the organization performing at the "Medium" level with significant room for improvement.

Define, scope, and validate the developer experience needs that the internal developer platform must address. Ensure needs are structured across the three DevEx dimensions, prioritized by cognitive load impact, and bounded by the Thinnest Viable Platform principle.

A structured developer experience needs discovery process is executed: cognitive load assessment categorizes load sources, feedback loop measurement establishes baselines, developer personas are documented with distinct need profiles, the TVP boundary is drawn using the CNCF's 13 capability domains, and acceptance criteria are defined with measurable targets. All stakeholder groups validate the resulting needs specification.

A coherent, prioritized set of developer experience needs is established with measurable acceptance criteria. The needs specification drives platform architecture decisions, golden path design, and roadmap prioritization. Developer experience measurement demonstrates sustained improvement as needs are progressively addressed.

alphas.name: Platform
alphas.description: The unified system of infrastructure, compute resources, networking, storage, delivery pipelines, observability, and foundational services that provides the technical foundation for developer self-service, aligned with the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model and designed to reduce developer cognitive load through progressive abstraction. In the IDP context, the platform is architected using recognized reference models (such as the Humanitec Five-Plane Architecture) with API-first design, continuous reconciliation, and infrastructure abstraction as core architectural principles.

states.name: Architecture Selected
states.description: The IDP's architectural vision, structural layers, and technology strategy are formally selected and agreed upon. The architecture defines the platform's capability planes, integration boundaries, and technology choices.

checklist.name: Reference architecture documented
checklist.description: The target platform architecture is documented using a recognized reference model. The Humanitec Five-Plane Architecture (Developer Control Plane, Integration/Delivery Plane, Monitoring/Logging Plane, Security Plane, Resource Plane) or equivalent provides the structural foundation.

checklist.name: API-first principles established

narratives.name: Platform Narrative
narratives.description: The platform maturity journey from initial architecture through organizational-scale operations.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations beginning their IDP journey typically operate at the Provisional or Operational level of the CNCF maturity model. Infrastructure provisioning is manual or template-based, security is gate-oriented, observability is fragmented, and developer self-service is limited. The CNCF maturity model assessment covers five aspects: Investment (funding model), Adoption (voluntary usage), Interfaces (self-service sophistication), Operations (reliability and scalability), and Measurement (data-driven decision making). Only 13.1% of organizations reach Optimizing; 45.5% operate at Operational.

The target maturity level should be determined per aspect based on organizational context. The CNCF explicitly warns: "reaching the highest level should not be a goal in itself. Each additional level of maturity is accompanied by greater requirements for funding and people's time." Most organizations should target Scalable (Level 3) for Interfaces and Operations, while Investment and Adoption may legitimately remain at Operational (Level 2) in smaller organizations.

The journey follows a progressive maturity path. Architecture selection and technology choices (months 1-3), core provisioning and first golden path (months 3-6), self-service readiness and early adopter onboarding (months 6-12), organizational scale and mature operations (months 12-24), and continuous evolution (ongoing). The DORA J-Curve predicts initial gains (basic automation), followed by a complexity dip (integration challenges, adoption friction), before recovery at higher performance levels.

Platform maturity is tracked through DORA metrics, CNCF maturity model self-assessment, developer adoption rate, platform SLO compliance, and developer satisfaction. Quarterly reviews assess progress against targets and adjust plans based on organizational reality. The measurement system guards against Goodhart's Law by using balanced, multi-dimensional metrics rather than optimizing for a single indicator.

narratives.name: IDP Essentials Baseline Narrative
narratives.description: The overarching narrative of the IDP Essentials baseline, framing the organizational journey from fragmented infrastructure to a mature internal developer platform.

narrativeContexts.context: The organization delivers software through a patchwork of team-maintained infrastructure. Each development team independently manages its own deployment pipelines, infrastructure provisioning, monitoring configurations, and security practices. Cognitive load from infrastructure management consumes approximately 45% of developer effort. New developers take weeks to become productive. Infrastructure costs are opaque and growing. Security reviews bottleneck delivery. Shadow IT proliferates as teams build workarounds. DORA metrics show the organization performing at Medium or below across all indicators. Developer satisfaction is low and declining, contributing to attrition in a competitive talent market.

A convergence of pressures creates an undeniable business case for change. Industry data validates that platform engineering has moved from experimental to mainstream: 55% of organizations use some form of platform engineering, 76% have dedicated platform teams, and Gartner projects 80% adoption by 2026. DORA 2025 research demonstrates that platform quality amplifies the impact of AI adoption on organizational performance. Developer retention data, competitive benchmarking, and executive recognition of infrastructure friction as a strategic impediment combine to trigger the decision to invest in an internal developer platform.

The platform engineering journey is a multi-year organizational transformation that challenges every assumption about how infrastructure should be delivered. The organization must: quantify the opportunity through developer experience research and build a compelling business case (Value focus), architect and build a platform with self-service capabilities, golden paths, and automated governance following the Thinnest Viable Platform principle (Solution focus), and restructure teams using Team Topologies, adopt platform-as-product practices, implement SRE principles, and manage the cultural transformation from project to product mindset (Endeavor focus). The DORA J-Curve predicts an initial performance dip as organizational complexity increases before recovering at higher levels. Resistance from developers skeptical of previous "platform" initiatives, infrastructure teams concerned about role changes, and security teams wary of reduced control must be addressed through demonstration of value rather than mandate.

The organization operates with a mature internal developer platform that delivers compounding returns across all three focuses. Developer cognitive load has shifted from 35/45/20 to approaching 50/15/35, with extraneous load dramatically reduced through self-service, golden paths, and automated governance. DORA metrics reach the High to Elite range. Developer NPS exceeds +40. Platform adoption exceeds 80% through voluntary preference, not mandate. The platform amplifies AI adoption impact and is recognized as a strategic asset. Platform engineering is an established discipline with career paths, community contribution, and industry recognition. The transformation sustains itself through embedded culture, continuous measurement, and product management discipline.

narratives.name: Platform Consumption Interface Narrative
narratives.description: The developer portal journey positioning the developer as hero and platform team as guide.

narrativeContexts.narrativeElementName: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeContexts.context: A new application developer (Hero) joins the organization and needs to deploy their first microservice. Without the developer portal, this involves: finding the right team wiki (which may be outdated), submitting infrastructure tickets (3-day turnaround), manually configuring CI/CD (inconsistent across teams), requesting security review (2-week queue), and debugging deployment issues (requires tribal knowledge from senior engineers). The Time to First Deploy is measured in weeks, not hours.

narrativeContexts.narrativeElementName: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeContexts.context: The developer portal (Guide) offers a clear, discoverable path: the software catalog shows all available platform services with documentation, the scaffolder creates a new project from a golden path template in minutes with CI/CD, security scanning, and observability pre-configured, self-service actions provision required infrastructure immediately, and deployment to staging happens automatically on merge. The portal embodies the plan: start simple, discover capabilities as needed, never fight the platform.

narrativeContexts.narrativeElementName: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeContexts.context: The developer deploys their first service to production within one day of joining. They voluntarily adopt the golden path because it eliminates friction they would otherwise encounter. Over the following weeks, they discover additional portal capabilities: the service catalog helps them find and consume team APIs, dashboards surface operational insights, and the CLI enables scripted automation. They contribute a documentation improvement through inner-source, becoming an active participant in the platform ecosystem.

narratives.name: Platform Asset Narrative
narratives.description: The workload lifecycle from identification through production operation on the platform.

narrativeContexts.context: A development team needs to build a new customer-facing API service. Under the pre-platform approach, this would require: requesting a Kubernetes namespace (2-day turnaround), configuring CI/CD from scratch (1-2 days of copy-paste-modify from another team), manually integrating observability (inconsistent between teams), requesting security review (2-week queue), and debugging production issues with ad-hoc tooling (requiring deep infrastructure knowledge). Total Time to First Deploy: approximately 3-4 weeks.
Create, deploy, and operate the API service using the internal developer platform's capabilities, demonstrating the workload lifecycle from identification through production operation.

The team selects a "REST API Service" golden path template from the developer portal. The scaffolder creates the project with CI/CD, security scanning, observability instrumentation, and documentation pre-configured. Self-service provisioning allocates a namespace with appropriate resource quotas, network policies, and secrets management. The first deployment to staging happens automatically on the initial merge. The service is registered in the service catalog with ownership and health information.

Time to First Deploy: 4 hours (from template selection to staging deployment). The service reaches production within 2 days with full observability, security compliance, and SLO monitoring. The team operates the service through platform dashboards and never needs to understand the underlying infrastructure. Support tickets: zero (self-service handled everything). The team's cognitive load shifts from infrastructure management to domain problem-solving.

narratives.name: Work Narrative
narratives.description: The platform work management journey from ad-hoc to product-centric delivery.

narrativeContexts.context: The platform team receives a steady stream of work requests: new golden path templates, infrastructure integrations, security policy updates, developer experience improvements, and operational incident response. Without product-centric work management, priorities shift based on who asks loudest, technical debt accumulates, and operational toil consumes an increasing share of team capacity.

Establish product-centric work management that balances capability development, operational toil reduction, developer experience improvement, and security governance. Ensure work delivers measurable developer value while maintaining platform reliability.

The platform team adopts product management practices: a backlog prioritized by developer impact, sprint cadence for capability delivery, explicit toil budget (capped at 50% per SRE principles), and quarterly planning aligned with developer experience research findings. Work intake is formalized to distinguish capability development from operational maintenance.

Delivery velocity becomes predictable. Developer-facing capabilities are delivered in regular increments with measurable adoption and satisfaction improvements. Operational toil decreases from 60% to 35% of team capacity through systematic automation. Stakeholders have clear visibility into platform roadmap and delivery progress.

checklist.description: The platform team's mission is articulated as an internal product team, not a shared infrastructure team. The mission centers on reducing developer cognitive load through self-service capabilities.

checklist.name: Scaling guidelines understood
checklist.description: Scaling guidelines are understood: 2-3 people for organizations with 50-100 developers (grassroots start), dedicated team at 100+ developers. 76% of enterprises report dedicated platform teams.

checklist.name: Team Topologies concepts introduced
checklist.description: Team Topologies concepts are introduced: the platform team is recognized as a distinct team type with specific interaction modes (primarily X-as-a-Service with consuming teams).

states.name: Formed
states.description: The platform team structure is established with clear responsibilities, interaction modes, and cognitive load boundaries. Team API contracts define expectations.

checklist.name: Dedicated team established
checklist.description: A dedicated platform team exists with a clear charter, fully allocated members, and centrally allocated budget. Members are not shared with other teams.

checklist.name: Team types defined
checklist.description: Team types are formally defined using Team Topologies taxonomy. The distinction between platform teams (build the platform), stream-aligned teams (consume the platform), enabling teams (facilitate adoption), and complicated subsystem teams (manage complex components) is operationalized.

checklist.name: Interaction modes documented
checklist.description: Interaction modes between teams are documented and agreed: Collaboration (temporary, time-boxed for capability co-creation), X-as-a-Service (stable, for mature capabilities), Facilitating (temporary, for onboarding and adoption support).

checklist.name: Team API defined
checklist.description: Team API contracts define expectations between the platform team and consuming teams: capabilities provided, support model, SLOs, feedback channels, and escalation paths.

checklist.name: Fractal structure designed
checklist.description: The platform team's fractal structure (sub-teams per capability domain) is designed for organizations at scale. Each sub-team owns a coherent set of platform capabilities with clear boundaries.

states.name: Collaborating
states.description: Teams work together effectively with deliberate interaction modes and cognitive load awareness. Collaboration interactions are time-boxed with planned transitions.

checklist.name: Collaboration interactions time-boxed
checklist.description: Initial platform capabilities are developed through time-boxed Collaboration with early adopter stream-aligned teams. Collaboration interactions have explicit transition plans to X-as-a-Service once capabilities stabilize.

checklist.name: Enabling teams facilitating
checklist.description: Enabling teams facilitate platform adoption through temporary coaching engagements. Enabling team members embed with consuming teams to build capability and reduce friction, then disengage once the team is self-sufficient.

checklist.name: Cognitive load assessed
checklist.description: Cognitive load assessment informs team boundary and interaction decisions. Team boundaries are drawn to respect cognitive load limits. Conway's Law is leveraged through the Inverse Conway Maneuver: team structure is designed to shape the desired platform consumption model.

checklist.name: Anti-patterns avoided
checklist.description: Common anti-patterns are identified and avoided: "everything is collaboration" (never transitioning to X-as-a-Service), "platform as ticket queue" (centralized bottleneck), "premature X-as-a-Service" (productizing before understanding consumer needs), and "shifting all burden onto the platform team."

states.name: Performing
states.description: Teams consistently deliver value with mature interaction patterns, high autonomy within guardrails, and balanced cognitive load distribution.

checklist.name: X-as-a-Service predominant
checklist.description: Platform consumption operates primarily in X-as-a-Service mode with clear, stable, self-service interfaces. Stream-aligned teams operate autonomously within platform guardrails.

checklist.name: Enabling engagements focused
checklist.description: Enabling team engagements are time-boxed and transition-focused. New team onboarding follows a structured program with measurable Time to First Deploy targets.

checklist.name: Continuous delivery without disruption
checklist.description: The platform team delivers continuous improvements without disrupting consuming teams. API stability, backward compatibility, and migration support are integral to the delivery process.

checklist.name: Cognitive load balanced
checklist.description: Cross-team cognitive load distribution is balanced. No team carries disproportionate cognitive burden. Developer satisfaction with team interactions exceeds organizational targets.

states.name: Adjourned
states.description: Teams are reorganized, disbanded, or repurposed as the platform initiative evolves. Knowledge transfer ensures organizational continuity.

checklist.name: Transitions planned
checklist.description: Team transitions are planned with comprehensive knowledge transfer. Documentation, operational runbooks, and architectural decision records are updated.

checklist.name: Organizational learning captured
checklist.description: Organizational learning from the team's experience is captured: what worked, what did not, and what should be done differently.

checklist.name: Service continuity maintained
checklist.description: If the platform team is restructured, the transition maintains service continuity for consuming teams. No capability gap is introduced during reorganization.

narratives.name: Team Narrative
narratives.description: The team journey from distributed infrastructure responsibility to Team Topologies-based organization.

narrativeContexts.context: Infrastructure management is distributed across development teams. Each team maintains its own deployment scripts, monitoring configurations, and security practices. There is no dedicated platform team -- infrastructure is everyone's part-time responsibility and no one's primary mission. Cognitive load is distributed unevenly, with senior engineers bearing disproportionate infrastructure burden.

The organization recognizes that distributed infrastructure management creates duplicated effort, inconsistent practices, and growing cognitive load. Industry data shows that 76% of enterprises with successful platforms have dedicated platform teams. The call is to establish a platform team as a distinct organizational unit with a product management mission.

Forming the platform team involves organizational challenges: identifying and recruiting platform engineers, establishing team boundaries and interaction modes, navigating the Collaboration-to-X-as-a-Service transition, managing resistance from teams whose autonomy is perceived as being reduced, and balancing platform standardization with team flexibility. The enabling team model must be established to support consuming team adoption without creating dependency.

The organization operates with a clear team topology: a platform team that builds and operates the IDP with product management discipline, stream-aligned teams that consume platform capabilities autonomously through self-service, enabling teams that facilitate adoption through time-boxed coaching, and cognitive load that is balanced across the organization. Teams collaborate deliberately, with explicit interaction modes and transition plans.

alphas.name: Way Of Working

In the IDP context, the Way Of Working integrates DevOps culture, Team Topologies framework, SRE practices, DORA metrics, and the platform-as-product paradigm into a coherent operating model.

checklist.name: Core principles documented
checklist.description: Core principles are documented: platform-as-product thinking, developer-as-customer, cognitive load reduction as design constraint, TVP as scope discipline, and the secure path as the easy path.

checklist.name: Industry methodology alignments declared
checklist.description: Industry methodology alignments are declared: DevOps culture (shared responsibility, continuous improvement), Team Topologies framework (team types, interaction modes, cognitive load), SRE practices (SLOs, error budgets, toil tracking), and DORA metrics (delivery performance measurement).

checklist.name: Ecosystem framing understood
checklist.description: The IDP ecosystem framing is understood: "The culture is DevOps. The framework for team design is Team Topologies. The team that builds developer experience is Platform Engineering. The role that protects reliability at scale is SRE. The empirical compass is DORA metrics."

checklist.name: Governance philosophy established
checklist.description: The governance philosophy is established: guardrails over gates, secure path as easy path, policy-as-code over manual review, and transparency over control.

checklist.name: Platform operating model defined

checklist.name: SRE practices selected

checklist.name: Developer workflow patterns documented

checklist.name: Product management practices active

checklist.name: Golden path usage growing

checklist.name: SRE practices operational
checklist.description: SRE practices are operational: incident response procedures are tested, SLO monitoring is active, toil is tracked and systematically reduced.

checklist.name: Enabling team support active

checklist.name: Platform-as-product driving evolution

checklist.name: Self-service as default

narratives.name: Way Of Working Narrative
narratives.description: The operating model journey from incoherent practices to integrated IDP operating model.

narrativeContexts.context: The organization's platform team operates without a coherent operating model. Infrastructure work is project-based with unclear priorities, operations consume most of the team's capacity, there is no systematic developer experience measurement, and governance operates through manual gates that bottleneck delivery. Consuming teams have inconsistent practices: some follow DevOps principles, others maintain traditional handoff-based workflows.

Establish a coherent Way of Working that integrates platform-as-product thinking, DevOps culture, SRE practices, Team Topologies interaction modes, and DORA measurement into a unified operating model for both platform and consuming teams.

The platform team adopts the IDP operating model: product management practices (user research, roadmap, adoption tracking), SRE principles (SLOs, error budgets, toil cap at 50%), GitOps workflows (declarative, version-controlled, continuously reconciled), and Team Topologies interaction modes (Collaboration for new capabilities, X-as-a-Service for stable capabilities, Facilitating for adoption support). DORA metrics and DXI surveys provide ongoing measurement.

The platform team operates as a high-performing product team. Operational toil decreases to 35% of capacity. Developer satisfaction NPS rises from -5 to +42. DORA metrics reach the High to Elite range across all indicators. Consuming teams voluntarily adopt golden paths and self-service capabilities. The operating model is recognized as a reference implementation within the industry.

alphas.name: Platform Governance
alphas.description: The automated controls, policies, guardrails, and governance mechanisms that constrain platform and workload behavior within organizational safety boundaries while maximizing developer autonomy and velocity. In the IDP context, governance follows the principle of enablement over restriction: golden paths make the right thing easy, guardrails make the wrong thing hard, and policy-as-code automates compliance so that manual gates are the exception rather than the rule.

states.name: Scoped
states.description: The need for platform governance is recognized and the scope of policy requirements is identified. The governance philosophy (enablement over restriction) is established.

checklist.name: Governance requirements inventoried
checklist.description: Governance requirements are inventoried across security, compliance, cost management, and operational standards. Critical versus non-critical policy areas are distinguished.

checklist.name: Governance philosophy established
checklist.description: The governance philosophy is established: enablement over restriction, automation over manual review. Google Cloud's control mechanism taxonomy is adopted: Golden Paths (recommended approaches), Guardrails (automated boundaries), Safety Nets (detection and recovery), and Manual Checkpoints (human review for exceptional cases).

checklist.name: Manual gate target established
checklist.description: The target state for manual gates is established: 5-10% of changes require human review. The remaining 90-95% are governed through automated policy enforcement.

checklist.name: Compliance framework selected
checklist.description: A compliance framework is adopted for the governance lifecycle. Microsoft's compliance framework provides a useful structure: "Start Right Templates" (golden paths with embedded compliance), "Stay Right Governance" (continuous automated enforcement), and "Get Right Campaigns" (remediation programs for non-compliant workloads).

states.name: Documented
states.description: Policies are formally defined and the policy-as-code approach is established. High-priority policies begin translation from documents to machine-readable code.

checklist.name: Policies formally documented
checklist.description: High-priority policies are formally documented with scope, rationale, enforcement requirements, exception criteria, and approval workflows.

checklist.name: Policy-as-code tooling selected
checklist.description: Policy-as-code tooling is selected: OPA/Rego for complex logic, YAML-based policies for simpler scenarios, and admission controllers for deployment-time enforcement.

checklist.name: Critical policies translated
checklist.description: Critical policies begin translation from documents to machine-readable code. The policy code undergoes the same review and testing processes as application code.

checklist.name: Exception workflow defined
checklist.description: Policy exception and approval workflows are defined for cases that cannot be handled through automation.

states.name: Enforced
states.description: Policies are actively enforced through automated mechanisms in CI/CD pipelines and at deployment time. Non-compliant configurations are prevented from reaching production.

checklist.name: Pipeline enforcement active
checklist.description: Policy-as-code enforces critical policies in CI/CD pipelines. Security scanning, compliance checks, and configuration validation run automatically as golden path pipeline stages.

checklist.name: Admission controllers deployed
checklist.description: Admission controllers prevent non-compliant workloads from reaching production. Rejected deployments receive clear remediation guidance explaining what is wrong and how to fix it.

checklist.name: Policy violations actionable
checklist.description: Policy violations generate clear, actionable remediation guidance. Developers can resolve most violations without platform team or security team involvement.

checklist.name: Golden paths embed compliance
checklist.description: Golden paths embed compliance requirements by default. A developer following a golden path is automatically compliant with organizational policies without additional effort.

states.name: Audited
states.description: Compliance is verified through continuous automated auditing with real-time visibility dashboards. Manual gates are actively being reduced toward the target.

checklist.name: Compliance dashboards operational
checklist.description: Compliance dashboards provide real-time visibility into governance status across all platform-managed workloads. Coverage gaps, policy violations, and remediation progress are visible.

checklist.name: Continuous auditing active
checklist.description: Policies undergo continuous automated auditing. Compliance status is verified in real-time rather than through periodic manual reviews.

checklist.name: Manual gates reduced
checklist.description: Manual security and compliance gates are actively being reduced toward the 5-10% target. Each manual gate is evaluated for automation potential.

checklist.name: Policy testing established
checklist.description: Policies undergo the same code review, testing, and deployment processes as application code. Policy changes are validated in non-production environments before enforcement.

states.name: Adaptive
states.description: The governance framework evolves adaptively based on organizational needs, regulatory changes, emerging threats, and operational data. Policies are continuously refined rather than statically maintained.

checklist.name: Policy evolution data-driven
checklist.description: Policy changes are driven by operational data: violation patterns, exception request analysis, remediation time trends, and developer friction metrics. Policies that create excessive friction without proportional risk reduction are refined.

checklist.name: Regulatory agility
checklist.description: New regulatory requirements are rapidly translated into automated policies. The governance framework accommodates regulatory change without requiring architectural changes.

checklist.name: Governance metrics tracked
checklist.description: Governance effectiveness is measured: percentage of automated policy coverage, manual gate usage rate, mean time to remediate violations, developer satisfaction with governance friction, and compliance audit findings.

narratives.name: Platform Governance Narrative
narratives.description: The governance maturity journey from manual gates to automated, adaptive policy enforcement.

narrativeContexts.context: Most organizations beginning their IDP governance journey rely on manual review gates for security and compliance. Change Advisory Boards review deployment requests, security teams manually audit configurations, and compliance is verified through periodic assessments. This model creates bottlenecks: security review queues of 2+ weeks are common, and developers work around governance rather than through it.

The target is automated governance where 90-95% of changes are validated through policy-as-code without human involvement. The investment rationale is compelling: automated governance is both faster (seconds versus weeks) and more comprehensive (every change is validated versus random sampling) than manual review. The target is not zero manual gates but minimal manual gates reserved for genuinely exceptional cases.

The journey progresses from policy documentation, through tooling selection and initial automation, to comprehensive pipeline and admission controller enforcement, and finally to adaptive governance that evolves with organizational needs. Investment includes policy engineering skills (OPA/Rego expertise), tooling infrastructure (admission controllers, policy engines), and organizational change (helping security teams transition from manual reviewers to policy engineers).

Governance maturity is tracked through metrics: policy automation coverage (percentage of changes validated automatically), manual gate frequency (target: below 10%), mean time to remediate policy violations, developer satisfaction with governance experience, and compliance audit findings. Course correction adjusts policies that create excessive friction without proportional risk reduction.

alphaInstances.name: Application Developer
alphaInstances.description: The primary consumer of platform capabilities. Evaluates the platform through the lens of cognitive load reduction, self-service availability, and impact on flow state. Represents the largest stakeholder group and the primary measure of platform success.

alphaInstances.name: Platform Engineer
alphaInstances.description: The producer who designs, builds, and operates platform capabilities. Evaluates the platform through engineering quality, operational sustainability, and technical debt. Straddles the producer-consumer boundary.

alphaInstances.name: Engineering Manager
alphaInstances.description: The organizational leader responsible for team productivity and delivery outcomes. Evaluates the platform through team velocity, DORA metrics, developer retention, and cognitive load distribution across teams.

alphaInstances.name: CISO / Security Officer
alphaInstances.description: The governance stakeholder responsible for organizational security posture and regulatory compliance. Evaluates the platform through policy enforcement coverage, supply chain security maturity, and audit readiness.

alphaInstances.name: Budget Owner
alphaInstances.description: The financial stakeholder responsible for platform investment decisions. Evaluates the platform through ROI, cost per developer, infrastructure efficiency, and strategic value enablement.

alphaInstances.name: Platform-as-Product
alphaInstances.description: The operating model treating the internal developer platform as an internal product with product management discipline: user research, roadmap prioritization, competitive analysis (against shadow IT), and value-driven evolution. The foundational cultural shift from project-based infrastructure delivery.

alphaInstances.name: DevOps Practice
alphaInstances.description: The cultural and technical practices bridging development and operations: continuous integration, continuous delivery, infrastructure-as-code, shared responsibility for production systems, and blameless post-mortems.

alphaInstances.name: SRE Practice
alphaInstances.description: Site Reliability Engineering practices applying software engineering to operations: SLOs with error budgets, toil tracking and reduction (capped at 50%), blameless post-mortems, and reliability engineering applied to developer-facing platform services.

alphaInstances.name: GitOps Workflow
alphaInstances.description: The operational model using Git as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and application configuration, with automated reconciliation (pull-based) maintaining desired state. Eliminates configuration drift through continuous reconciliation.

alphaInstances.name: Inner Source
alphaInstances.description: The practice of applying open-source collaboration patterns within the organization: consuming teams contribute improvements to platform capabilities through pull requests, code review, and community governance. Extends platform development beyond the platform team's direct capacity.

activitySpaces.name: Explore Possibilities
activitySpaces.description: Explore the possibilities presented by the creation of a new or improved internal developer platform. In the IDP context, exploration includes assessing developer productivity gaps, benchmarking against industry maturity models (CNCF, DORA), evaluating competitive pressure from shadow IT alternatives, and identifying strategic opportunities such as AI enablement through platform quality.

activitySpaces.name: Assess and Monitor Value
activitySpaces.description: Conduct rigorous business analysis to quantify potential ROI of the IDP investment, map platform capabilities to developer productivity improvements, and secure executive sponsorship through data-driven business cases.

activitySpaces.name: Monitor Value Realization
activitySpaces.description: Track KPIs including DORA metrics, DX Core 4 framework, developer adoption rates, and infrastructure cost efficiency to proactively manage bottlenecks and demonstrate continuous ROI of the IDP investment.

activitySpaces.name: Manage Platform Economics
activitySpaces.description: Define chargeback/showback models, right-size infrastructure through FinOps practices, optimize costs, and transition from project-based to product-centric funding for the internal developer platform investment.

activitySpaces.name: Understand Stakeholder Needs
activitySpaces.description: Conduct developer experience research using validated instruments (DXI, SPACE), utilize Jobs-to-be-Done frameworks to understand developer motivations, and ensure the platform demonstrates value through product management practices.

activitySpaces.name: Ensure Stakeholder Satisfaction
activitySpaces.description: Provide internal marketing, create developer feedback loops, deliver accessible support, and build platform communities of practice to ensure continuous voluntary adoption by development teams.

activitySpaces.name: Establish Secure Guardrails
activitySpaces.description: Shift security left into development and delivery pipelines, embed zero-trust principles, codify compliance requirements into policy-as-code, implement SLSA framework for supply chain security, and ensure secure-by-default platform operations through golden path security integration.

activitySpaces.name: Define Platform Capabilities
activitySpaces.description: Distill developer experience research findings into actionable requirements, apply the three DevEx dimensions (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state) as requirement categories, and define the Thinnest Viable Platform scope to avoid over-engineering.

activitySpaces.name: Architect and Build the Foundation
activitySpaces.description: Establish the IDP's architectural foundation using reference models (Humanitec Five-Plane Architecture), implement declarative provisioning, build CI/CD pipelines with embedded security, configure control plane patterns with continuous reconciliation, and instantiate core platform services.

activitySpaces.name: Operate and Evolve the System
activitySpaces.description: Execute Day-2 operations using SRE practices (SLOs, error budgets, toil tracking), manage platform observability across infrastructure and workloads, ensure high availability of developer-facing services, and continuously evolve the platform based on operational data and developer feedback.

activitySpaces.name: Develop the Golden Paths
activitySpaces.description: Build golden path templates, developer portal interfaces (web portal, CLI, API), and automated scaffolding that reduce cognitive load and enable autonomous developer self-service across the full application lifecycle from Day-1 creation through Day-2 operations.

activitySpaces.name: Integrate Toolchain Services
activitySpaces.description: Specify, provision, and securely integrate workloads into the platform ecosystem, ensuring seamless interoperability with established golden paths, observability infrastructure, security controls, and the developer portal.

activitySpaces.name: Prepare To Do The Work
activitySpaces.description: Prepare the platform work for execution by organizing backlogs, decomposing work items, allocating capacity, validating architectural alignment, and ensuring TVP principle adherence.

activitySpaces.name: Manage Work Execution
activitySpaces.description: Coordinate platform delivery cycles using product management cadence, allocate engineering capacity, track delivery velocity, manage technical debt, and ensure predictable platform capability development.

activitySpaces.name: Support the Team
activitySpaces.description: Define team structures using Team Topologies principles (four team types, three interaction modes), establish cognitive load as the primary design constraint for team boundaries, and manage the Collaboration-to-X-as-a-Service transition for platform capabilities.

activitySpaces.name: Stop The Work
activitySpaces.description: Plan and execute team dissolution, knowledge transfer, and member reassignment when platform teams are restructured or repurposed as the IDP initiative evolves.

activitySpaces.name: Establish Way Of Working
activitySpaces.description: Define and implement the platform operating model: SRE practices (incident response, SLOs, error budgets, blameless post-mortems), GitOps workflows (declarative, version-controlled, continuously reconciled), developer workflow patterns (golden paths, self-service), and feedback loop mechanisms (surveys, retrospectives, metrics).

activitySpaces.name: Implement Policy-as-Code
activitySpaces.description: Translate manual governance rules into automated, machine-readable policies (OPA/Rego, YAML-based policies, admission controllers) that execute within delivery pipelines and at deployment time without impeding developer velocity.

activitySpaces.name: Stop The Work
activitySpaces.description: Stop platform work and close out completed endeavors with outcome validation, knowledge transfer, and value communication to stakeholders.

activitySpaces.name: Decommission and Retire
activitySpaces.description: Safely decouple, deprecate, and remove obsolete platform capabilities, legacy infrastructure, retired workloads, or outdated operational practices to minimize technical debt and resource waste.

activitySpaces.name: Curate Developer Experience
activitySpaces.description: Systematically research, measure, and optimize the holistic developer experience across feedback loops, cognitive load, and flow state dimensions, driving platform improvement through evidence-based developer needs discovery.

activitySpaces.name: Manage Service Discovery
activitySpaces.description: Create and maintain a centralized, navigable registry of platform capabilities, services, and APIs that enables developers to discover, understand, evaluate, and consume available platform offerings.

activitySpaces.name: Secure Software Supply Chain
activitySpaces.description: Implement and operate software supply chain security practices including build provenance, artifact signing, dependency management, SBOM generation, and enhanced scrutiny for AI-generated code, embedded into the platform's delivery pipelines.

activitySpaces.name: Measure Platform Adoption
activitySpaces.description: Track, analyze, and report on platform adoption patterns, maturity progression, and value delivery to inform investment decisions, demonstrate ROI, and identify improvement opportunities.

activitySpaces.name: Enable Platform Onboarding
activitySpaces.description: Execute structured programs that enable new developers and teams to become productive on the internal developer platform efficiently, combining automated environment setup, guided first-project experiences, and temporary enabling team facilitation.
